title: Cytron Maker Pi RP2040 Board Explorer
alt: Pinout diagram of the Cytron Maker Pi RP2040 robotics board, with colored leader lines pointing from printed labels to each connector, button, LED, and port on the purple circuit board.
prompt: Hover over any part of the board, or over its printed label, to learn what it does. Or pick a part below.

zones.label: Vin Terminal
zones.summary: This green screw terminal is one way to power your robot. Loosen the two screws, slide in the bare wires from a battery pack, and tighten them down.
facts: It accepts any power source from 3.6 V to 6 V, such as a pack of four AA batteries (about 6 V).
Match your wires to the − and + marks printed below the terminal.
Your DC motors and servos run on this same voltage, so fresh batteries mean faster motors.
zones.tip: Never connect a 9 V battery here. Anything over 6 V can damage the board. Cytron also suggests using either Vin or a LiPo battery, not both at once.

zones.label: LiPo Battery Connector
zones.summary: This small white socket takes a single-cell LiPo or Li-ion battery. LiPo stands for lithium polymer, a light, flat, rechargeable battery that is perfect for robots.
facts: A single-cell LiPo battery supplies about 3.7 V.
Plug a USB cable into the board's Micro USB port to recharge the battery right on the board.
A built-in protection circuit keeps the battery from overcharging or draining too far.
Your code can check the battery level: GP29 (ADC3) reads half of the battery voltage.
zones.tip: Check that the battery's red wire lines up with the + mark before you plug it in. Some batteries are wired backward! If the board won't turn on with a new battery, charge it first to wake up the protection circuit.

zones.label: Power LED
zones.summary: This small light, marked PWR, turns on whenever the board has power. It is the first thing to check when your robot seems dead.
facts: LED stands for Light-Emitting Diode, a tiny part that glows when current flows through it.
It lights up no matter where the power comes from: USB, a LiPo battery, or the Vin terminal.
zones.tip: No light? Check the On/Off switch first, then your battery or USB cable.

zones.label: On/Off Switch
zones.summary: Slide this switch to turn the board's power on or off.
facts: Switching off stops the motors right away, so it works as an emergency stop.
Your program is saved in the board's flash memory. It is still there when you switch back on.
zones.tip: Switch the board off before you plug in or unplug motors, servos, or sensors.

zones.label: Micro USB Port
zones.summary: This is how your computer talks to the robot. Plug in a USB cable to upload programs from Thonny, and the same cable can also power the board.
facts: USB power also recharges a LiPo battery plugged into the LiPo connector.
When you flash MicroPython, the board shows up on your computer as a USB drive named RPI-RP2.
zones.tip: Use a data USB cable, not a charge-only cable. If your computer can't see the board, try a different cable first. It's the most common reason uploads fail.

zones.label: Debug Port
zones.summary: These three pins are a special debugging port for the RP2040 chip. Professional debugging tools plug in here to pause the chip and look inside while a program runs.
facts: The pins are SWCLK, GND, and SWDIO. SWD stands for Serial Wire Debug.
You don't need this port for MicroPython. Thonny talks to the board over USB instead.
zones.tip: Advanced makers can use a second Raspberry Pi Pico as a low-cost debug probe on this port.

zones.label: RP2040 Microcontroller
zones.summary: This square chip is the brain of your robot. The RP2040 runs your MicroPython program, reads the sensors, and decides what the motors should do. It is the same chip that is on a Raspberry Pi Pico.
facts: It has two processor cores that run at up to 133 MHz (133 million steps per second).
It has 264 KB of RAM for your running program, plus 2 MB of flash memory on the board to store your files.
Because it's the same chip, the MicroPython firmware made for the Raspberry Pi Pico works on this board.
This board has no WiFi or Bluetooth. Our wireless robots use a Robo Pico board with a Pico W instead.
zones.tip: The chip isn't labeled on the diagram, but everything else on the board exists to power it, protect it, or connect it to the world.

zones.label: Crystal
zones.summary: This silver oval is a crystal that keeps time for the RP2040. A tiny slice of quartz inside vibrates exactly 12 million times per second.
facts: The RP2040 uses these steady ticks as its heartbeat and multiplies them up to its much faster running speed.
Accurate timing is what makes sleep(1) last exactly one second and keeps USB communication working.
zones.tip: This part isn't labeled on the diagram. Quartz crystals are also what keep time in most watches and clocks.

zones.label: DC Motor Terminals
zones.summary: These two black screw terminals connect your robot's two DC (direct current) gear motors. Each motor has two wires, and each wire gets its own screw.
facts: Motor 1 is controlled by GP8 (M1A) and GP9 (M1B).
Motor 2 is controlled by GP10 (M2A) and GP11 (M2B).
In most of our kits' config.py files, Motor 1 is the right wheel and Motor 2 is the left wheel.
Each motor can draw 1 A all the time, or up to 1.5 A for bursts shorter than 5 seconds.
zones.tip: Motor spinning the wrong way? Swap its two wires in the terminal. You don't need to change any code.

zones.label: Motor Status LEDs
zones.summary: These four tiny lights show what the motor driver is doing. Each light turns on when its motor output is switched on.
facts: An MxA light means that motor is being driven forward. An MxB light means backward.
The real direction depends on how you wired the motor, so "forward" is just a starting guess.
The lights work even when no motor is connected.
zones.tip: Debugging trick: lift your robot off the table and watch these lights while your code runs. You can see exactly what your program is telling each motor.

rects.note: M2A light (Motor 2 forward) and M1B light (Motor 1 backward)

zones.label: Motor Test Buttons
zones.summary: Press one of these four buttons to spin a motor at full speed. You don't need any code, so they are perfect for checking your wiring first.
facts: M1A runs Motor 1 forward, and M1B runs it backward.
M2A runs Motor 2 forward, and M2B runs it backward.
The motor runs only while you hold the button down.
zones.tip: Hold your robot in the air before you press a test button. At full speed, it can zoom right off the table!

zones.label: Motor Driver Chip
zones.summary: This black chip is the motor driver. An RP2040 pin can only supply a tiny current, so this chip works like a set of heavy-duty switches that send real battery power to the motors.
facts: Inside are two H-bridges. An H-bridge is four switches that can send current through a motor in either direction.
Your code controls it with GP8 and GP9 (Motor 1) and GP10 and GP11 (Motor 2).
PWM, or Pulse Width Modulation, flicks the power on and off very fast to set the speed. This chip handles PWM up to 20 kHz.

table.caption: What the motor does for each pair of input pins

zones.tip: Never wire a motor straight to a GPIO pin. The pin can't supply enough current and could be damaged. Driving motors is this chip's job.

zones.label: Servo Ports
zones.summary: These pins connect up to four RC servo motors. A servo is a motor that turns to an exact angle, which is great for grippers, arms, or a sensor that looks left and right.
facts: The four servo signal pins are GP12, GP13, GP14, and GP15, one for each column.
Each port has three pins: S (signal), + (power), and − (ground).
Servo power equals your power source voltage.
zones.tip: Plug the servo cable in with its signal wire (usually orange, yellow, or white) on the S row. The brown or black wire goes on the − row.

zones.label: GPIO Status Indicator LEDs
zones.summary: This row of 13 tiny lights, marked DIGITAL IO STATUS, shows the state of the GPIO pins wired to the Grove ports. A light turns on when its pin is HIGH (3.3 V) and off when the pin is LOW (0 V).
facts: Each light's pin name is printed right below it: GP0 to GP7, GP16, GP17, and GP26 to GP28.
You can watch a digital output change without adding any parts.
I2C data lines rest HIGH, so their lights often glow when an I2C sensor is plugged in.
zones.tip: Quick test: turn a pin on and off from the REPL and watch its light blink.

zones.label: Grove Ports
zones.summary: These seven white 4-pin connectors let you plug in Grove sensors and modules with a single cable. Each port has GND, 3.3 V power, and two signal pins.
facts: Grove 4 (GP16 and GP17) is the I2C bus the Base Bot uses for its distance sensor. I2C is a two-wire bus that many sensors can share.
Grove 5, 6, and 7 have analog pins that read changing voltages, like a light sensor's output.
Grove 5 and Grove 6 share GP26, so don't plug two different sensors into both.
zones.tip: All the Grove ports together can supply only 300 mA at 3.3 V. That's plenty for sensors, but never power a motor from a Grove port.

zones.label: Piezo Buzzer
zones.summary: This square black part makes beeps, tones, and even simple songs. Inside is a thin crystal disk that bends when voltage is applied, pushing the air to make sound.
facts: It is connected to GP22, which is SPEAKER_PIN in our config.py.
Your code picks the pitch by setting the PWM frequency. For example, 440 Hz plays the note A.
A higher frequency makes a higher-pitched sound.
zones.tip: Use beeps as signals: one beep when the robot starts, two beeps when it sees an obstacle.

zones.label: Buzzer Mute Switch
zones.summary: Slide this switch to silence the piezo buzzer without changing your code. It is a lifesaver in a classroom full of beeping robots!
facts: Muting only stops the sound. Your program keeps running normally.
The speaker symbols printed beside the switch show the sound-on and mute positions.
zones.tip: If your code plays a tone but you hear nothing, check this switch first.

zones.label: RGB LEDs (NeoPixel WS2812)
zones.summary: These two bright lights can glow in almost any color. Each one has a red, a green, and a blue LED inside, and your code mixes them.
facts: Both lights share one pin, GP18, which is NEOPIXEL_PIN in our config.py.
They are chained together: LED 0 is first in line and LED 1 is second.
Each color goes from 0 (off) to 255 (full brightness). Red 255, green 0, blue 255 makes purple.
NeoPixel is a nickname for the WS2812 smart LED, which has a tiny controller chip built in.
zones.tip: Use colors to show what your robot is doing, such as green for driving and red for "obstacle ahead!"

zones.label: Programmable Buttons
zones.summary: Your program can read these two push buttons. Use them to start a routine, switch modes, or pick a speed.
facts: The buttons are connected to GP20 and GP21. The pin names are printed above each button.
Your code checks whether each button is pressed. This is called a digital input because it has only two states.
zones.tip: Try this: make your robot wait until you press the GP20 button before it starts driving. No more robots racing off the moment you switch them on!

zones.label: Reset Button
zones.summary: Press this button, marked RST, to restart the RP2040, just like switching it off and back on. Your program starts again from the beginning.
facts: Resetting does not erase your code. The program saved on the board runs again.
It is handy when your program gets stuck or your robot acts strangely.
zones.tip: Reset is quicker than the power switch, and you don't have to unplug anything.

zones.label: Boot Button
zones.summary: This button puts the board into its special firmware-loading mode. It does the same job as the BOOTSEL button on a Raspberry Pi Pico.
facts: Hold BOOT, press and release RST, then let go of BOOT. The board shows up on your computer as a USB drive named RPI-RP2.
Drag a MicroPython UF2 file onto that drive to install MicroPython. The board restarts by itself when it's done.
The board comes from the factory with CircuitPython, so you flash MicroPython once before using our kits.
zones.tip: You don't press BOOT for everyday coding. It's only for installing or updating firmware.

quiz.question: You want to test Motor 1's wiring by spinning it forward, without writing any code. What do you press?
quiz.explanation: The M1A motor test button runs Motor 1 forward at full speed while you hold it.

quiz.question: Where do the two wires from a DC gear motor attach?
quiz.explanation: Each motor's two wires go into one of the black screw terminals.

quiz.question: Your robot is up on a block and your code sets GP8 HIGH. Which lights show you the driver is trying to spin Motor 1?
quiz.explanation: The M1A motor status light turns on when Motor 1 is being driven forward.

quiz.question: Where would you plug in a small, flat, rechargeable 3.7 V battery?
quiz.explanation: A single-cell LiPo battery plugs into the LiPo connector and recharges over USB.

quiz.question: Your code plays a tone, but the room stays silent. Which part should you check first?
quiz.explanation: The mute switch silences the buzzer even while your code keeps running.

quiz.question: Which part makes sound when your code sends a PWM signal on GP22?
quiz.explanation: The piezo buzzer on GP22 turns PWM frequencies into tones.

quiz.question: Which chip actually runs your MicroPython program?
quiz.explanation: The RP2040 microcontroller is the brain of the board, the same chip as on a Raspberry Pi Pico.

quiz.question: Where do you plug in the cable that uploads programs from Thonny?
quiz.explanation: The Micro USB port carries your programs from the computer and can power the board.

quiz.question: You need to install MicroPython. Which button do you hold so the board shows up as the RPI-RP2 drive?
quiz.explanation: Hold BOOT while pressing RST to enter the firmware-loading mode.

quiz.question: The Base Bot's distance sensor uses I2C on GP16 and GP17. What kind of connector does its cable plug into?
quiz.explanation: GP16 and GP17 come out on Grove 4, one of the seven Grove ports.

quiz.question: Which part could you light up purple by setting red 255, green 0, and blue 255 on GP18?
quiz.explanation: The two NeoPixel RGB LEDs on GP18 mix red, green, and blue.

quiz.question: Your program is stuck in an endless loop. Which button restarts it?
quiz.explanation: The reset button restarts the RP2040 without erasing your saved program.

quiz.question: Which part lets your program wait for a person to press GP20 before driving?
quiz.explanation: The programmable buttons on GP20 and GP21 are digital inputs your code can read.

quiz.question: Where can you connect up to four RC servo motors?
quiz.explanation: The servo ports use GP12 to GP15 for their signal pins.

quiz.question: You want to power the robot from a 4 x AA battery pack with bare wires. Where do the wires go?
quiz.explanation: The green Vin screw terminal accepts 3.6 V to 6 V from bare wires.

quiz.question: Which row of tiny lights shows whether each Grove pin is HIGH or LOW?
quiz.explanation: The 13 DIGITAL IO STATUS lights turn on when their pins are HIGH.

quiz.question: Which light tells you the board is getting power?
quiz.explanation: The PWR light turns on whenever the board is powered.

quiz.question: Which chip holds the two H-bridges that let your robot drive in reverse?
quiz.explanation: The motor driver chip contains two H-bridges, one for each motor.

quiz.question: Which part vibrates 12 million times per second to keep time for the RP2040?
quiz.explanation: The quartz crystal gives the RP2040 a steady timing heartbeat.
